title: Desire and respect
hookLine: seeing others as souls, not objects
tomorrow: five thieves, Simran says. is there a medicine for each?

cards: The group chat lights up at lunch. Someone has posted photos of girls from the junior class, with scores underneath. The jokes come fast.
Simran stares at her screen, and her face goes hot. One of the photos is Maya's little sister. Her thumb hovers.
She could leave the chat. She could laugh it off. Or she could say something, and be the one who ruined the fun.
Her lunch goes cold. Maya is at the next table, laughing about something else, and doesn't know yet.

teach.h: KAAM: A PERSON MADE A THING.
teach.b: The Sikh word for this thief is kaam: desire that's lost its respect, wanting that turns a person into a thing. It's the first name in the list of five thieves on ang 600.
In the Sukhmani, on ang 274, Guru Arjan describes a devoted person as one whose eyes don't gaze on another's beauty with craving.

teach.h: ANG 274: THE WORK IS IN THE EYES.
teach.b: Notice where he puts the work: in the eyes. Not in a rule about clothes, or a list of places to avoid. In how we look.
Desire itself isn't the thief; Sikh teaching honors love and marriage. The thief is the look that strips someone down to a score. And the medicine is in the eyes too.
Sheikh Farid says, on ang 1381, in paraphrase: the Creator is in the creation, and the creation lives in God, so whom can we call bad?
Guru Gobind Singh, in the Akal Ustat, has a line Sikhs repeat: recognize the whole human race as one.

So see the soul. Here's the line worth repeating: a score is something you give a person; a soul is something they already have. Simran types: that's my best friend's sister, and half these girls are my friends.
Take it down. A pause. Then one boy writes: yeah, fair.
The photos disappear. Her hands are shaking a little, and she lets them. She never tells Maya's sister.

how: Sikhs name lust (kaam) as one of the five thieves; Sikh teaching honors love within marriage and asks that everyone be seen with respect, as carrying the same divine light.

o: seeing other people as souls, not as objects
never noticing whether anyone is attractive
keeping your opinions about people to yourself

games.q: the eyes and the soul — tap the pairs.
p: desire that turns a person into a thing
eyes that don't gaze with craving
the Creator is in the creation
the whole human race as one

s: Sikh teaching treats all desire as the thief
desire itself isn't the thief; Sikh teaching honors love and marriage. the thief is the look that makes a person a thing.
Guru Gobind Singh wrote that the whole human race should be recognized as one
a line from the Akal Ustat that Sikhs repeat.
staying out of it is the respectful choice when others are rating people
seeing the soul can mean speaking up; Simran asked them to take it down.

games.q: a coworker shows you a dating profile and starts mocking how the person looks. everyone at the table is laughing. what fits today's line?
o: say something that turns the person back into a person.
laugh along quietly so the moment passes faster.
say nothing now, but think less of your coworker.
games.why: a score is something you give a person; a soul is something they already have. Simran asked them to take it down, and one boy wrote: yeah, fair.

practice: Let your eyes rest on a face: someone near you, a photo of someone you know, or your own reflection. Instead of judging anything, look for what you can't see, a worry they carry, a hope, a story only they know.
Then lower your gaze and breathe, still holding that person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Desire and respect. Kaam, the thief that turns a person into a thing, and eyes that see the soul instead.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kaam, lust or desire without respect, the first of the five thieves named on ang 600.

carryVoice: See the soul: a score is something we give; a soul is already there. Talk soon.

sources.ref: Ang 600 (Sorath, Mahala 3: the five thieves, beginning with kaam), paraphrased
Ang 274 (Gauri Sukhmani, Mahala 5: par triaa roop na pekhai netr), paraphrased
Ang 1381 (Salok Farid: khaalak khalak mahi, khalak vasai rab maahi; mandaa kis no aakheeai), paraphrased
Akal Ustat (Dasam Granth), Guru Gobind Singh: maanas kee jaat sabhai ekai pahichaanbo, paraphrased
